name: NoSQL & Data Stores
description: Document, key-value, wide-column, graph, search and time-series stores — what each is for and what each gives up.

modules.name: Store Families
modules.description: The five main NoSQL shapes and the workloads they were built for.

cards.prompt: Name the main NoSQL families and a representative of each.
cards.answer: Key-value (Redis, DynamoDB), document (MongoDB, Couchbase), wide-column (Cassandra, HBase, Bigtable), graph (Neo4j, Neptune), search (Elasticsearch, OpenSearch) and time-series (InfluxDB, TimescaleDB, Prometheus).
cards.explanation: 'NoSQL' describes what they are not. What actually differs is the data model, the query capability and the consistency guarantee — pick by access pattern, not by label. Many of them have since added SQL-ish query languages.

cards.answer: Documents embed related data for single-read access; relational normalises and joins at query time.
cards.explanation: Embed when the data is read and written together and bounded in size; reference when it is shared, unbounded or independently updated. Schema-less really means schema-on-read: the schema still exists, it just lives in your application code.

cards.prompt: Why does DynamoDB modelling start from access patterns rather than entities?
cards.answer: Because you can only query efficiently by partition key (and optionally sort key). There are no joins and no ad-hoc queries, so the table layout has to be designed around the exact reads you will perform.
cards.explanation: This produces single-table designs where several entity types share a table with composite keys. The pay-off is predictable single-digit millisecond latency at any scale; the price is that a new access pattern may require a new index or a backfill.

cards.prompt: Beyond caching, what is Redis actually good at?
cards.answer: Rate limiting (atomic counters with TTL), distributed locks, leaderboards (sorted sets), session storage, queues and streams, pub/sub, and set operations for tags and recommendations.
cards.explanation: The value is atomic operations on rich data types in a single-threaded command loop — no race conditions between check and set. Remember it is primarily in-memory: persistence (RDB/AOF) exists but Redis is not your system of record.

cards.prompt: When is a graph database genuinely better than SQL with join tables?
cards.answer: When queries traverse variable-depth relationships — shortest path, 'friends of friends of friends', fraud rings, dependency chains. Each hop in SQL is another join written at authoring time; a graph traversal expresses depth as a parameter.
cards.explanation: Graph engines store adjacency directly, so a hop is a pointer walk rather than an index lookup. For fixed one- or two-hop relationships, a relational schema is usually simpler and faster. Postgres recursive CTEs cover many cases without a new database.

modules.name: Distribution & Consistency
modules.description: CAP, replication, partitioning and what 'eventually consistent' means in practice.

cards.prompt: State the CAP theorem precisely, and the common misreading.
cards.answer: When a network partition occurs, a distributed system must choose between consistency (linearisability) and availability. The misreading is 'pick two of three' — partitions are not optional, so the real choice is CP or AP *during a partition*.
cards.explanation: PACELC extends it usefully: else (no partition), you trade latency against consistency. That is why 'eventually consistent' stores still offer strong reads at higher latency, and why quorum settings (R + W > N) are a per-query decision in Cassandra and DynamoDB.

cards.prompt: Why is `current_date` a terrible partition key for a high-write table?
cards.answer: Every write for a given day lands on one partition — a hot shard that limits throughput to a single node while the rest idle.
cards.explanation: Good partition keys have high cardinality and even access distribution. Fixes: prefix with a hash or a bucket number, use a compound key such as `(user_id, date)`, or add a random suffix and fan out reads. Monotonic keys (timestamps, sequential IDs) hot-spot for the same reason.

cards.answer: Synchronous acknowledges only after replicas have the write (no data loss, higher latency); asynchronous acknowledges immediately (fast, but a failover can lose recent writes).

left.title: Synchronous
points: A slow replica can stall writes

right.title: Asynchronous
points: Failover may lose the tail of the log

cards.explanation: Replication lag is why a user can write a comment and not see it on the next page load if that read hits a replica. Fixes: read-your-writes routing to the primary for a window, or session consistency tokens.

cards.prompt: What does a user actually experience under eventual consistency, and how do you make it acceptable?
cards.answer: Stale reads, and occasionally seeing their own write disappear. Mitigate with read-your-writes (pin the session to the primary or the same replica briefly), optimistic UI, and monotonic-read guarantees so time never appears to run backwards.
cards.explanation: 'Eventually' has no bound by default — measure and alert on replication lag. Some data tolerates staleness (view counts) and some does not (account balance, permissions); classify per field, not per system.

cards.prompt: A new service needs a datastore. What is the sensible default, and what justifies moving off it?
cards.answer: Start with Postgres. Move off it when you have a specific, measured need it cannot meet: petabyte-scale writes, sub-millisecond key-value latency, full-text relevance ranking, graph traversal depth, or genuinely global multi-master writes.
cards.explanation: Postgres covers relational, JSONB documents, full-text search, geospatial, time-series (Timescale) and queues adequately. One well-understood system beats three half-understood ones, and 'we might need scale later' is not a measurement.
